_note: WhatsDaf's own English renderings of the Hebrew commentaries on Sefaria (Vilna edition). Keys are <commentary>:<amud><segment>.<comment>. Square brackets are our clarifications. Very long Tosafot are condensed and marked "In brief".
rashi:a1.1: To exclude Rabbi Yosei: of our mishna.
rashi:a1.2: In a place where there is no Sage: but where there is a Sage, he alone releases it.
rashi:a2.1: Who, for example: would that Sage be?
rashi:a2.2: By inference, those two may be anyone?: [This is said] in astonishment. That is, even if the two are amei ha’aretz; and how are amei ha’aretz fit to join [the court]?
rashi:a2.3: Who are made to understand: the reasons of the halakhot of vows, and they understand; and that Sage will teach the two.
rashi:a3.1: Lest you say: we hold in tractate Gittin (67a) that Rabbi Yosei, “his reasoning is with him,” so let the halakha be in accordance with him.
rashi:a3.2: Nimmuko: his reason. For he would bring a reason for his statements at all times.
rashi:a4.1: Resolve from this: from what Rav Ḥananel said in the name of Rav, “The halakha is not in accordance with Rabbi Yosei,” resolve that the earlier statement, which Rav Yehuda said above, uncertain whether in the name of Rav or in the name of Shmuel, “Three permit the firstborn,” was stated in the name of Shmuel. For if it were in the name of Rav, why would Rav need to say twice that three permit the firstborn and that the halakha is not in accordance with Rabbi Yosei?
rashi:a6.1: Mishna. One who slaughters the firstborn: and sold some of its meat.
rashi:a6.2: And it became known that he did not show it: to a Sage.
rashi:a6.3: What they ate: the buyers ate.
rashi:a6.4: And he returns the money to them: as a penalty, since it was a doubtful prohibition.
rashi:a6.5: The meat must be buried: for an unblemished firstborn is prohibited for benefit.
rashi:a7.1: They sold it: the buyers [sold it] to gentiles. Since he did not cause them [to eat] a prohibition, they pay him the price of tereifa meat, which is cheap, and he returns the remainder to them.
rashi:a9.1: Gemara. Katza: is repulsed, as in “and I abhorred [va’akutz] them” (Leviticus 20[:23]).
rashi:a9.2: He returns to them all the money: for nothing of what they ate is of benefit to them, from the moment it became known to them.
rashi:a9.3: He deducts: and so he takes a little [of the money]? [This is said] in astonishment.
rashi:a10.1: And let him say to him: the Israelite to the priest who sold [it]: What loss did I cause you? Had the meat been in your hand, it would have required burial, since you slaughtered it unblemished.
rashi:a11.1: For example, where he sold him: the priest who slaughtered [it sold] the place of the blemish to the Israelite.
rashi:a11.2: For he says to him: the priest [says]: Had it been in my hand, I would have shown it [to a Sage] as it is, slaughtered.
rashi:a11.3: In accordance with Rabbi Yehuda: as we say in chapter Ad Kama (above, Bekhorot 28a): One who slaughters the firstborn and afterward shows its blemish, Rabbi Yehuda permits.
rashi:a12.1: Untithed produce: why does he take a little? [Because] the seller can say to the buyer: Had you not eaten them, I would have remedied them.
rashi:a12.2: Libation wine: why does he take a little? [And it answers:] for example, where he did not sell him the libation wine itself, but mixed it with kosher wine and sold them. He can say to him: Had you returned it to me, I would have sold it to gentiles, except for the value of the libation wine in it.
rashi:a15.1: Mishna. For these blemishes: [Rashi gives only the opening words of the new chapter.]
rashi:a15.2: The ḥasḥus: the cartilage [tenukh] of the ear, which is called (Rashi adds an Old French gloss).
rashi:a15.3: But not from the skin: for it becomes healthy again and is not a blemish. And this “skin” is the soft lobe of the ear.
rashi:a15.4: [On the wording:] Damage [pegima] does not occur without something missing, but “split” implies even without something missing.
rashi:a16.1: Gemara. But why? Lame and blind are written: [as the blemishes] for which one may slaughter a firstborn, and not anything else, as it is written: “And if there be any blemish therein, lame or blind,” and adjacent to it: “You shall eat it within your gates,” that is, without sacrifice.
rashi:a17.1: And it answers: “If there be any blemish therein” is also written: which implies other blemishes as well.
rashi:a19.1: And it also desists from its labor: for example, a lame animal is kept from walking and a blind one from seeing.
rashi:a19.2: Why then did we learn: “its ear was damaged” is a blemish? But it is not kept from hearing!
rashi:a20.1: It is an amplification: for “any” [kol] is written, and we do not expound it by [the rule of] generalization and detail.
rashi:a20.2: If so: that it is an amplification, let one slaughter for hidden blemishes as well.
rashi:a20.3: Gums: (Rashi adds an Old French gloss).
rashi:a20.4: External: those in the middle of the mouth.
rashi:a20.5: That were damaged: that were slightly lacking.
rashi:a20.6: That were scratched [shenigmemu]: that were cut across their width with a knife, and nothing was lacking, but [it is] like a split.
rashi:a20.7: The internal: (Rashi adds an Old French gloss).
rashi:b1.1: [A hidden blemish] is not called an ill blemish: only an exposed one, which makes it unsightly [is called so].
rashi:b1.2: If so: that “any blemish” is an amplification.
rashi:b2.1: Now, we do not redeem on account of it: [we do not redeem] disqualified consecrated animals [for a temporary blemish].
rashi:b2.2: Will we slaughter on account of it: a firstborn outside [the Temple]?
rashi:b3.1: When it says: [in] another verse: “And if it be of an impure animal, then he shall redeem it according to your valuation” [Leviticus 27:27].
rashi:b5.1: If so: that animals with a temporary blemish are also redeemed, what did “lame and blind” accomplish? For they imply permanent blemishes and not temporary ones.
rashi:b6.1: By the hand of Heaven: that it was born with it.
rashi:b7.1: Shetaḥgor: that a fingernail catches in it, if one checks [it] the way one checks a knife.
rashi:b9.1: Rather, of the first tanna and Rabbi Yosei: for a karshina is only slightly larger than a lentil.
rashi:b10.1: The sol: a sliver with a sharp point, which is called (Rashi adds an Old French gloss).
rashi:b10.3: The makdei’aḥ [gimlet]: (Rashi adds an Old French gloss).
rashi:b11.1: So too, anything of metal: and in the first chapter of Kiddushin [21b] it explains their dispute: Rabbi expounds [by the rule of] generalizations and details, and Rabbi Yosei expounds [by the rule of] amplifications and restrictions.
rashi:b13.2: How does he become blemished?: it heals!
rashi:b13.3: Rather, they pierce only: [read] as a statement [not a question]. Certainly they pierce only in the upper part of the ear, which is cartilage. And in any case it is difficult, for it teaches here that the piercing makes him blemished, and Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Yehuda says that piercing can be done with a needle, [whose hole] is not as large as a lentil.
rashi:b14.1: Here for slaughtering, there for disqualifying: there are many blemishes in a firstborn that disqualify it from being offered on the altar but do not make it fit to be slaughtered, as we learned: “These are [the blemishes] for which one does not slaughter, neither in the Temple nor in the country,” etc. [41a].
rashi:b15.1: Hinda: by this name they knew it; and in the vernacular (Rashi adds an Old French gloss).
rashi:b16.1: Karshina: [is it one] that stands tightly in the hole, so that even though it does not enter and exit through it, it is a blemish? Or perhaps it is not a blemish until the hole is wide enough for a karshina to enter and exit through it?
rashi:b16.2: I heard [a ruling] similar to it: we derive it from the end [of the passage], where he says: “We learned: a drill and its obstruction,” which means entering and exiting [38a].
rashi:b17.1: The spine and the skull: when whole, they impart impurity in a tent, while other bones do not impart impurity in a tent. And how much must they be lacking so that they do not impart impurity?
rashi:b18.1: This is the reading: “And Rav Ḥisda was sitting and raising a dilemma …” and “It was stated: Rav Safra said: [It was] a shmaata [an amoraic statement] that Rav Taḥlifa said to Rav Ḥisda, that thus Shmuel taught him.”
rashi:b19.1: And your mnemonic: so that you do not err as to who said “a shmaata” and who [said] “a baraita”: “Rav Yehuda bar Shmuel teaches” [so Rashi’s text reads here; he goes on to name Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda], for we find in many places in the Talmud that Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda speaks in the language of a baraita: “Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda taught,” in tractate Avoda Zara, [in the passage on] remedies, in chapter Ein Ma’amidin (28b).
rashi:b20.1: And he said to him: Rav Ḥisda to Rav Taḥlifa.
rashi:b20.2: If so: that Beit Hillel said “like a sela,” you have made Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel one.
rashi:b20.3: A window: an opening not made by human hands, where the wall between one house and another fell away a little by itself.
rashi:b20.4: Its measure: for bringing impurity from this house to that house.
rashi:b20.5: The size of a large fist: since it was not made by human hands, anything less than this is not significant.
rashi:b20.6: Ben Avatiaḥ: the name of a man who was very fleshy.
rashi:b20.7: And it is: [the size of] that fist.
rashi:b21.1: Of the chamber: that was kept in the chamber for drilling whatever was needed for the Temple’s upkeep.
rashi:b21.2: Like the Italian pundeyon and like a Neronian sela: that is, it resembles both this and that.
rashi:b21.3: And it is: [the size of] that sela and that pundeyon.
tosafot:a1.1: They dissolve [mefirin] the vow: he used the language of the verse [hafara]; but for a Sage the term hattara [release] applies. And so too in chapter HaMokher et HaSefina (Bava Batra 74a), concerning the Divine Voice, it says: “And now that I have sworn, who will annul [mefer] it for Me?”
tosafot:a2.1: “Rabbi Yehuda says: One of them is a Sage. By inference, those [others] are anyone? Ravina said: Who are made to understand and do understand”: so it is written in most books. And some books read: “Who, for example? Rav Naḥman said: For example, me,” and it appears from the language of the Kuntres [Rashi] that he read so. But it is difficult: how, then, does it object, “By inference, those [others] are anyone”? Say no; rather, [they need only be] less than Rav Naḥman! And if you ask: according to the other reading too, from where does it know [that they may be] anyone? Perhaps by inference those [others] are less than an expert, but not just anyone! One can answer: it is obvious to it that Rabbi Yehuda’s Sage is not like the Sage mentioned above, which refers to an expert, for even Rabbi Yehuda agrees that a single expert releases a vow; and here, since he is not speaking of an expert, what standard does he set for the others? But it is still difficult: if so, from where does it know that [the ruling of three] comes to exclude Rabbi Yehuda? Since Rabbi Yehuda is not speaking of an expert, perhaps Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Abba [so Tosafot’s text; the daf reads Rav Ḥiyya bar Amram] agrees that we require one of them to be like Rabbi Yehuda’s Sage. And it is forced to say that “three dissolve a vow” implies to it that all three are equal.
tosafot:a9.1: And libation wine: even though in the third chapter of Horayot (11a) it says that one who [eats] it ordinarily is a heretic with regard to libation wine, as with carcasses, nevertheless it is not counted as something one is repulsed by. And furthermore, here we conclude [that it is] by way of a mixture.
tosafot:a15.1: Mishna. From the ḥasḥus: it means cartilage [tenukh], as in “the tips of the wings and the ḥasḥot” in chapter Keitzad Tzolin (Pesaḥim 84a); and “a piece of an ear” (Amos 3[:12]) is rendered [in the Aramaic translation] “ḥasḥus de’udna.”
tosafot:a18.1: In brief: Tosafot note that the same exposition, “exposed blemishes that do not return,” is used in the first chapter of Kiddushin (24b) for the tooth and eye that free a slave. They ask: why, then, is a fallen tooth not a blemish in an animal, since it is exposed and does not grow back? [For below, in chapter Mumin Elu (Bekhorot 44a), a priest whose teeth were removed is disqualified only for appearance, since he is not equal among Aaron’s offspring, which implies that an animal is fit; and even a person is not disqualified for one tooth; and for an animal the Gemara here counts only damaged or scratched external gums and extracted internal ones, not lost teeth.] They answer that a slave is different, since the verse revealed it; but here, since teeth normally fall out with age, it is not like lameness and blindness. They note that another reason is still needed, since the eyes too [fail] with age. They ask further: why does striking a slave on the ear and deafening him count there as an exposed blemish that does not return, so that he goes free, while in chapter Elu Mumin (Bekhorot 45b) we learned that a deaf-mute and an imbecile are disqualified in a person and fit in an animal, and in a person only because he is not equal among Aaron’s offspring? They answer that for a slave the Merciful One revealed that even a slight thing counts as a blemish to go free, for he goes free for his tooth. Open on Sefaria for the full text.
tosafot:b1.1: Extracted, yes; damaged or scratched, no: it could have cited the case below, which explicitly lists among “these are the ones for which one does not slaughter, neither in the Temple nor in the country” internal gums that were damaged or scratched. But it preferred to cite the inference from the first clause, which shows that even though in the external [gums] it is an exposed blemish, in the internal ones it is not a blemish.
tosafot:b2.1: Now, we do not redeem on account of it, etc.: And if you ask: according to this first answer, that a temporary blemish is excluded by an a fortiori argument, what does “lame and blind” accomplish? One can answer: it holds now that if “lame and blind” were not written, we would include a temporary blemish from “any ill blemish,” and I would have said that it comes to exclude [the conclusion of] the a fortiori argument; and we would also not exclude hidden blemishes from “ill blemish.”
tosafot:b11.1: To include anything taken by hand: in the first chapter of Kiddushin (21b) it explains [that this is] because he expounds amplifications and restrictions: “and you shall take” amplified, “awl” restricted, “through his ear” amplified again. What did it amplify? It amplified everything. What did it restrict? It restricted a caustic drug. And it is puzzling: if from “and you shall take” we include anything taken by hand, and a drug is not called “taken by hand,” why do I need amplification, restriction and amplification? From the wording “and you shall take” alone, only something taken by hand would be included! One can answer: he does not expound it from the wording “and you shall take”; rather, this is what it means: [it serves] to include anything taken by hand, because we expound amplifications and restrictions.
tosafot:b14.1: Here for slaughtering, there for disqualifying: since it disqualifies a priest, it implies that it is a Torah-level blemish. And perhaps the reason one does not slaughter [for it] is that it is not clearly visible, and we decree on account of hidden blemishes. Alternatively, the reason it disqualifies a priest is that he is not equal among Aaron’s offspring. Alternatively, it is a temporary blemish, and we require that he not be disqualified even temporarily, since it is written: “[And he shall return] to his family,” which we expound in Kiddushin (ibid.) [to mean]: to that which is permitted in his family [i.e., to his family’s standing].
tosafot:b17.1: In brief: Tosafot explain, citing the first chapter of Eruvin (7a), that by Beit Shammai’s measure, a drill’s hole, the person would also die, and that the same applies to tereifa; the measures refer to both the spine and the skull, and Beit Hillel come to say that by their view a drill’s hole is more than “enough that if removed from a living person he would die.” They discuss Rabbeinu Tam, who explains that “and likewise for tereifa” does not refer to the skull, since at the beginning of Elu Tereifot (Ḥullin 42b) the Gemara objects from a deficiency in the spine but not from one in the skull (a perforated brain membrane alone makes an animal tereifa, without any deficiency), and who explains that Eruvin (7a) calls the rulings on the spine and the skull two contradictory stringencies because they disagreed over tereifa in a person, who is more resilient and is not rendered tereifa by a perforated membrane without a deficiency. Even by his explanation, Tosafot say, one must explain as they did, that at Beit Shammai’s measure he dies, as at Beit Hillel’s. They reject his proof from Ḥullin: a deficiency may render an animal tereifa only because the membrane will eventually be perforated, like a lung that looks like ink or kohl (Ḥullin 47b). They also question his distinction between people and animals from Ḥullin (43a), where the Gemara objects from Job (“He pours out my gall upon the ground,” and Job lived), and suggest he could have explained instead that the case is a perforated upper membrane only: in an animal the lower membrane is soft and does not protect the brain, while in a person it is hard and protects it, so a person needs a deficiency as well; but where the two are alike, there is no distinction at all. Open on Sefaria for the full text.
gershom:a1.1: To exclude Rabbi Yehuda: [for here] we do not require one of them to be a Sage.
gershom:a2.1: Who are made to understand and do understand: so that they are not complete amei ha’aretz.
gershom:a3.1: Resolve from this: since this was stated in the name of Rav, learn from it that the earlier one, of which we said it was uncertain whether in the name of Rav or in the name of Shmuel, is certainly Shmuel’s. For if that one too were in the name of Rav, and here too Rav said the halakha is [not] in accordance with Rabbi Yosei [the printed text lacks “not”], but that even three members of the synagogue permit, that is the same as the earlier one; why would he need to say it twice? No: certainly only one was stated in the name of Rav, and the other by inference; it was stated by inference from that one, according to Rav.
gershom:a4.1: And he returns the money to them: for the Rabbis penalized him.
gershom:a5.1: They return the meat to him: for it is permitted for benefit, since he may sell it to a gentile.
gershom:a6.1: The buyers sold the meat to a gentile at a high price, or cast it to the dogs, and have not yet paid the money: they pay him the value of a tereifa, which is cheap, and do not pay him all the money they received for it, because he sold a tereifa of his own accord.
gershom:a7.1: He deducts from the money for them, corresponding to what they ate, and returns the rest.
gershom:a8.1: A firstborn: why should he deduct from the money? Let the buyer say to him: What loss did I cause you by eating it? For had I returned it to you, there would be no remedy; it would be buried. [The answer:] for example, where he sold that limb that had a blemish, and he ate it; and therefore he deducts from the money.
gershom:a9.1: For he says to him: Had you not eaten it, I would have shown it to a Sage and he would have permitted it to me.
gershom:a10.1: In accordance with Rabbi Yehuda: who permits examining a blemish after slaughter, as we said in the chapter above.
gershom:a11.1: Untithed produce: he can say to him: Had you not eaten [it], I would have remedied them; therefore he deducts. And libation wine: [wine] that is not libation wine alone, but became libation wine through a mixture, and he sold it to him; had he returned it to him, it would have been permitted for benefit, in accordance with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, as we learned, etc. Therefore he deducts.
gershom:a13.1: For these blemishes. The ḥasḥus: which is called in the vernacular (Rabbeinu Gershom adds an Old French gloss).
gershom:a14.1: The size of a karshina: as much as [allows] the insertion of a karshina seed.
gershom:a15.1: Why are they slaughtered for these blemishes?
gershom:a16.1: Lame and blind: alone are written.
gershom:a17.1: “If there be any blemish therein” is also written, unspecified: it included these.
gershom:a18.1: And it desists from its labor: lame and blind, which are not fit for labor.
gershom:a19.1: Why then did we learn: “its ear was damaged”? For on that account it does not desist [from labor], and yet it is a blemish.
gershom:a20.1: “Any ill blemish” is an amplification: and it includes these.
gershom:a21.1: Gums: the external gums are a blemish when they are scratched, because it is not hidden, since it is visible when it eats.
gershom:b1.1: I require: that an ill blemish be visible, and there is none. That is, these are internal; if they were not actually extracted, it is not an ill blemish, since it is not visible.
gershom:b2.1: If so, a temporary blemish: which is visible, should count as an ill blemish, and one should slaughter for it. Why then did we learn: “and not from the skin,” etc.?
gershom:b3.1: A temporary blemish is logical reasoning: that one should not slaughter for it; for now that we do not redeem for a temporary blemish, will we slaughter, etc.? And if you wish, say: if so, that one may slaughter for a temporary blemish, what does it help to write “lame and blind”? Rather, learn from it that one slaughters only for a permanent blemish, like lame and blind.
gershom:b4.1: Rather, of the first tanna and Rabbi Yosei son of (HaMeshullam) [Yehuda] [the text is corrected so in brackets]: between a karshina and a lentil there is only a little [difference].
gershom:b5.1: The sol: (Rabbeinu Gershom adds an Old French gloss).
gershom:b6.1: Only in the milat: in the flesh beneath the ear. Rather, they pierce only in the upper part of the ear, in the cartilage, and there the priest becomes blemished. And Rabbi Yosei includes even a needle for the piercing, and with it a Hebrew slave who is a priest becomes blemished [the printed text garbles “Hebrew slave”; it is corrected in brackets]. Evidently a hole smaller than a lentil is a blemish.
gershom:b7.1: It is not difficult; here for slaughtering: for this, the firstborn is slaughtered only for a hole the size of a lentil.
gershom:b8.1: There for disqualifying: from being sacrificed, even a hole [made] by a needle disqualifies.
gershom:b9.1: Hinda: in his place they call a karshina “hinda.”
gershom:b10.1: A karshina that stands tightly in the hole, or that enters and exits freely?
gershom:b11.1: How much deficiency in the spine, so that it does not impart impurity in a tent?
gershom:b12.1: And likewise in the skull. Shmaata: that is, a statement, this one of Shmuel.
gershom:b13.1: And your mnemonic, for the reading: “Rav Yehuda said: a baraita” [so Rabbeinu Gershom’s text]: for we often find “Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda taught,” and the baraita [version] is the main one.
gershom:b14.1: He said to him: Rav Ḥisda [said]: If so, as you say, a sela, you have made the words of Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel one, as we learned: A window not made by human hands, for example a wall between two houses, with impurity in one house, and in that wall there is a hole like a window that came about by itself, for example a stone that became perforated by itself: the measure of that hole, if it is like a large fist, brings the impurity from house to house, and the people and vessels in the other house become impure. And if the window is less than this, it blocks the impurity.
gershom:b15.1: The fist of Ben Batiaḥ: the son of the sister of Rabban Yoḥanan ben Zakkai, who was an exceptionally large man.
gershom:b16.1: And it is: the measure of that fist is like a large head.
gershom:b17.1: And a window that was made by human hands, that someone drilled: its measure, if it is the size of the large drill of the chamber, like the large drill that was in the chamber, it brings the impurity; and since it was made by human hands intentionally, a smaller measure suffices. Evidently, the drill too is like a sela; if so, what is [the difference] between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel regarding the skull?
